A, B and C are Truth, Lie and Random in an unknown order. Truth always answers truthfully, Lie always falsely, and Random may answer yes or no arbitrarily. They understand the questions and know each other’s types. Using three yes/no questions, identify all three.

Use N(Q): “If I asked you Q, would you say yes?” For a non-random person, N(Q) answers Q truthfully. Ask A N(“Is B Random?”). If yes, choose X=C; if no, choose X=B. X is certainly non-random: if A is Random both others are safe; otherwise its normalized answer excludes Random. Ask X N(“Is A Random?”). If yes, A is Random; if no, the unchosen member of B and C is Random. Finally ask X N(“Are you Truth?”). If yes, X is Truth; if no, X is Lie. The remaining non-random person has the opposite type.

Ten discs of different sizes are stacked largest to smallest on one of three pegs. Move them to another peg, moving one top disc at a time and never placing a larger disc on a smaller one. What is the minimum number of moves?
1,023. To move n discs, move n−1 aside, move the largest, then move n−1 onto it: T(n)=2T(n−1)+1, with T(1)=1. Thus T(10)=2¹⁰−1.

A, B, and C are each either always truthful or always lying. A says, “B is truthful.” B says, “C is lying.” C says, “A and B are different types.” Which type is each person?

In 8,549,176,320, each digit occurs once. What ordering rule do the English names of those digits follow?

I keep rain out of a house from above, yet I am not an umbrella. Chimneys may rise through me. What am I?

A tank contains 100 fish. Ten die but remain in the tank. Fifteen other fish are removed, and five of those are returned. Counting living and dead fish, how many are now in the tank?

A lily pad doubles in size every day. It takes 48 days to cover the entire pond. How long did it take to cover half the pond?
47 days. On day 47 it covered half — then doubled on day 48 to cover it all.
A girl has as many brothers as sisters. Each brother has half as many brothers as sisters. How many children are there in total?
7 children: 4 girls and 3 boys. Each girl has 3 brothers and 3 sisters. Each boy has 2 brothers and 4 sisters.
You overtake the person in 2nd place in a race. What place are you in now?
2nd place. You took their position — you did not overtake 1st place.
In this puzzle, each egg needs exactly five minutes once placed in boiling water. A large pot keeps boiling normally with five eggs in it. If all five go in together, when are they ready?

Lina, Sami, and Noor each chose a different drink: tea, coffee, or juice. Sami chose coffee, Noor did not choose juice, and Lina did not choose tea. Who chose each drink?

Three books—red, green, and blue—stand in a row. The red book is to the left of the green book, and the blue book is to the right of the green book. What is their order from left to right?
Three umbrellas are red, blue and green. Amal does not own the red or blue one. Sami owns the blue one. Which color is Amal’s umbrella?

A towel, a comb and a key are on a table. The item Noor used absorbed water from her wet hands. Which item did she use?
A box contains two red balls and one blue ball. Without looking, how many balls must you take to guarantee having a red ball?
Two. At most one drawn ball can be blue.
A library has four floors numbered 1–4. History is above Science, Science is on floor 2, and History is not on floor 4. Which floor holds History?
Floor 3. It is the only floor above 2 other than 4.
Ali, Badr and Huda have different pets: a cat, a dog and a bird. Ali has the bird. Badr does not have the dog. Who has the cat?

A light starts off. You press a switch five times; each press reverses its state. Is it on or off at the end?
On. Odd-numbered presses turn it on; even-numbered presses turn it off.
When I was 6 my sister was half my age. Now I am 70. How old is my sister?

A two-digit number has digits that add to 11. Reversing its digits makes the number 27 greater. What is the original number?
47. If the tens digit is a and the ones digit is b, then a+b=11 and 9(b−a)=27, so b−a=3. Thus a=4 and b=7.
A three-digit vault code has distinct digits. The first digit is twice the third, the middle digit is one greater than the third, and all three digits add to 13. What is the code?
643. Let the third digit be t. The digits are 2t, t+1, and t, so 4t+1=13 and t=3.
Is 8% of 50 the same as 50% of 8?
Yes, both equal 4. In general, x% of y always equals y% of x.

You drive 60 miles to a shop at a constant 20 mph and return along the same 60-mile route at 60 mph, with no stops. What is your average speed for the whole journey?

Among 4, 6 and 8, which number equals the sum of its positive divisors smaller than itself?
6: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. For 4 the sum is 3, and for 8 it is 7.
I am a father. Another man’s only son is my son’s father. Who am I to that other man?
His son. The man's only son is my son's father — meaning I am that son.

A treasure is in exactly one of three boxes. Box 1 says, “The treasure is in Box 2.” Box 2 says, “The treasure is not in Box 2.” Box 3 says, “The treasure is not in Box 1.” Exactly one note is true. Which box holds the treasure?

Three deliveries are made on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. Food arrives before books; books arrive before clothes. On which day do the books arrive?

Four cards show A, D, 4 and 7. Each has an English letter on one side and a number on the other. To test “If the letter is a vowel (A, E, I, O or U), the number is even,” which cards must you turn over?
A and 7. Turn A to check for an even number, and 7 to make sure there is not a vowel on its other side. D and 4 cannot disprove the rule.
A seller claims a coin was minted in 44 BCE. Its original inscription, he says, labels the year “44 BC” using the modern BC dating convention. What contradicts his claim?
That dating convention was introduced later. Such an inscription cannot be original to a coin minted in 44 BCE, though a later commemorative coin could use it.
Three talks—AI, Design, and History—must fill slots 1, 2, and 3. AI is before Design, Design is not in slot 3, and History is not in slot 1. What is the schedule?
Slot 1: AI; slot 2: Design; slot 3: History. No other ordering satisfies all three constraints.
A cube is painted on all six faces and cut into 27 equal smaller cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
12. Each of the cube's 12 edges has one non-corner small cube, and each such cube has exactly two painted faces.
In a class of 30 students, 18 study Arabic, 14 study English, and 5 study neither language. How many study both Arabic and English?
7. Twenty-five students study at least one language, so the overlap is 18 + 14 − 25 = 7.
I am an even positive integer and have exactly two positive divisors. Why must I be 2?
Any even number greater than 2 has the distinct divisors 1, 2 and itself. Only 2 has exactly two: 1 and 2.
Exactly two of four lamps A, B, C, and D are lit. A and B are in opposite states, C is in the same state as A, and D is off. Which lamps are lit?
A and C. If A were off, only B would be lit, contradicting the condition that exactly two lamps are lit. Therefore A and C are on, while B and D are off.

A car is placed uniformly behind one of three doors. You choose one. The host knows its location, always opens an unchosen goat door, and always offers a switch to the other closed door. Does always switching or always staying win more often?
Switching wins with probability 2/3; staying wins with probability 1/3. Switching wins exactly when the initial choice was wrong.
100 lockers are all closed. Person 1 opens all; person 2 toggles every 2nd; person 3 toggles every 3rd... Which lockers remain open after all 100 people?
The perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100. Only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors, so they end up open.

In an idealized two-child model, each child is independently equally likely to be a boy or girl. A family is selected at random from those with at least one boy, without inspecting a particular child. What is the probability of two boys?

A robot travels 1 metre, then half a metre, then a quarter, and keeps halving each new distance forever. What total distance does the sequence approach?
2 metres. If S = 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + …, then S/2 = 1/2 + 1/4 + …; subtracting gives S/2 = 1.
An ant sits on one corner of a 1×1×1 cube. What is the shortest path along the surface to the opposite corner?
√5 ≈ 2.236. Unfold two faces into a flat 1×2 rectangle — the straight line across is √(1² + 2²) = √5.

Exactly one of two paths is safe. Two guards know which one: one always answers truthfully and the other always lies. Both know the other’s rule. What single yes/no question to either guard lets you choose the safe path?
Ask: “Would the other guard say the left path is safe?” If yes, go right; if no, go left. Either guard gives the opposite of the truth about the left path.
Two fathers and two sons go fishing. They each catch exactly one fish, yet only three fish are caught in total. How?

A statement says, “This statement is false.” In classical two-valued logic, what contradiction follows from assuming it is true?

Every red token in a bag is round. Some tokens in the bag are red. Must at least one token in the bag be round?

A snail is at the bottom of a 10-metre well. Each day it climbs 3 metres and each night slips back 2 metres. How many days does it take to escape?

A photo session starts at 18:10 and lasts 35 minutes. Dinner starts 20 minutes after the session ends. When does dinner start?
19:05. The session ends at 18:45; adding 20 minutes gives 19:05.

Three switches outside a room control three initially off incandescent bulbs inside. The bulbs become warm when on and remain detectably warm briefly after switching off. You may safely inspect light and residual warmth, but enter only once. How can you match switches to bulbs?

100 prisoners may agree on a plan before isolation. A lamp starts off. One prisoner visits its room at a time and may change the lamp. Everyone is selected repeatedly without limit. How can one prisoner eventually know with certainty that all have visited?

Only the counter turns it off, counting each such event. At 99 signals, all have visited. Repeated selection guarantees eventual completion.
Each term describes the runs of identical digits in the preceding term. What follows 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221?

Twelve balls are labelled 1–12. Exactly one has a different mass; the other eleven have the same mass. You do not know whether the odd ball is heavier or lighter. Give three balance-scale weighings and a complete rule to identify the odd ball and its type.

You have two ropes, each taking exactly 1 hour to burn, but with non-uniform burning rates. How do you measure exactly 45 minutes?
Light rope 1 at both ends and rope 2 at one end simultaneously. When rope 1 finishes (30 min), light rope 2's other end. When rope 2 finishes = 45 minutes total.
On an island, every person is either a knight (always tells truth) or a knave (always lies). You meet two people, A and B. A says: 'At least one of us is a knave.' What are A and B?
A is a knight and B is a knave. If A were a knave, his statement ('at least one is a knave') would be true — a contradiction. So A is a knight telling the truth, which means B must be the knave.
What is the last digit of 7¹⁰⁰?

A convex polygon has n vertices. From each vertex, exclude that vertex and its two neighbors. Derive the number of diagonals, making sure not to count each diagonal twice.
Each vertex connects diagonally to n−3 vertices, giving n(n−3) endpoint counts. Each diagonal has two endpoints, so the number is n(n−3)/2.
Every object in a collection has property P. Every object with P has Q. An object lacks Q. Can it belong to that collection?

For the same transmitted power, higher voltage permits lower current. Resistive heating loss is I²R, so reducing current reduces those losses.
Why must survey teams coordinate alignment when tunnel excavation advances from opposite ends?
To make the two headings meet at the required horizontal position and elevation rather than miss each other.
What is a pile foundation and when is it used?
A deep foundation using slender elements installed by driving, boring, or other methods. Loads transfer through shaft resistance, end bearing, or both when shallow foundations are unsuitable.
What is the purpose of a camber in road design?
A slight convex curvature across the road surface that drains rainwater to the sides, improving safety and surface longevity.
What is a combined sewer overflow, and why can it pollute receiving waters?
During heavy rain, a combined sewage-and-stormwater system may discharge excess flow before full treatment, releasing sewage and other pollutants into receiving waters.
What is the difference between a simply supported beam bridge and a continuous beam bridge?

A simply supported span rests independently between two supports. A continuous beam extends across more than two supports, so neighboring spans share bending effects; actual reactions depend on loading and geometry.
What is the water hammer effect in pipelines?
A transient pressure surge caused by a rapid change in flow, such as sudden valve closure. Surge-control vessels and controlled valve operation can help limit it.
What is the difference between AC and DC in power transmission?

AC reverses direction periodically and is easily transformed to different voltages, ideal for grid transmission. DC flows constantly in one direction and is more efficient for very long distance (HVDC) or submarine cable transmission.
What is a breakwater in harbor engineering?
A structure built in open water to absorb or deflect wave energy, protecting harbor facilities, vessels, and coastlines from wave action and erosion.
What is the purpose of expansion joints in concrete bridges and roads?
Intentional gaps that allow concrete to expand in heat and contract in cold without cracking or buckling due to thermal stress.
What is the function of a cell tower base station in mobile networks?
It receives and transmits radio signals between mobile devices and the core network. Each tower covers a geographic cell; as users move, connections hand off to the next tower seamlessly.
What is a bascule (drawbridge) and how does it work?
A movable bridge section that pivots upward like a seesaw to let tall ships pass. A counterweight on one end reduces the force needed to raise the movable span.
In a horizontal venturi meter under steady incompressible flow with small losses, why is pressure lower at the narrow throat?
Continuity requires higher speed at the throat; Bernoulli's energy balance then gives lower static pressure there.
What is the difference between a metro (subway) and a light rail system?

A metro runs on fully grade-separated, dedicated track — usually underground or elevated — with high frequency and capacity. Light rail may share road space, runs at surface level, carries fewer passengers, but costs less to build.

What guidance does an Instrument Landing System (ILS) provide to an approaching aircraft?
Radio-based lateral guidance from the localizer and vertical guidance from the glideslope. ILS guidance alone does not mean the aircraft lands automatically.
What is the California Bearing Ratio (CBR) test used for in road construction?
It measures a soil's load-bearing capacity by comparing the pressure to penetrate a soil sample versus a standard crushed rock, determining whether ground can support pavement layers.
What is structural redundancy and why is it important in infrastructure?
Providing alternative load paths or components so a local failure need not cause total system failure. Whether a particular failure is tolerated depends on the design and remaining capacity.
What is a cascading failure in an electrical grid?
An initial outage changes power flows and can overload or trip other elements, whose loss triggers further outages.
What is induced demand in transportation planning?
Additional travel stimulated by increased road capacity or reduced travel cost. It can consume part or much of the initial congestion relief; the size of the effect depends on context.
What is non-revenue water (NRW) and why does it matter for utilities?

The difference between water put into a distribution system and water billed to customers — including leaks, pipe bursts, meter errors, and theft. In many cities NRW exceeds 30% of production, representing significant revenue loss and resource waste.
What is structural health monitoring (SHM) and how is it applied to bridges?
Measuring structural behavior and condition using sensors such as strain gauges, accelerometers, and corrosion sensors, to help detect changes that warrant engineering assessment.
What are pumped-storage hydropower plants and why are they valuable to power grids?

They pump water uphill during excess electricity periods, then release it through turbines during peak demand — acting as large-scale rechargeable batteries, the most mature form of grid-scale energy storage.
What is the aim of perpetual asphalt pavement design?
To preserve long-life structural layers while periodically renewing the surface. It limits damaging strains in deeper layers; it does not promise an infinite maintenance-free lifespan.
What is the difference between a dry bulk terminal and a liquid bulk terminal in port design?

Dry bulk handles loose solids (coal, grain) using conveyors and grab cranes. Liquid bulk handles petroleum, chemicals, or LNG using pipelines, pumps, and tanker berths with spill containment. Each requires completely different handling infrastructure.
What is the 'water-energy nexus' in infrastructure planning?
Water systems need energy for pumping, treatment, and distribution; energy systems may need water for cooling, hydropower, and fuel production. Planning one therefore affects the other.
What does explicit service-life design add to a purely prescriptive materials specification?

It evaluates deterioration, exposure, maintenance, and performance against a stated service-life target. Prescriptive codes can also include assumed design lives, but may not explicitly model each project's deterioration.
What is critical infrastructure interdependency and why does it complicate resilience planning?

Power, water, transport, and telecoms systems are deeply interdependent — power outages disable water pumps; telecom failures disrupt emergency response; transport breakdowns prevent maintenance. Restoring one system often requires another to already work, creating cascading failure risks that require holistic resilience modelling.

What is the Arabic term for Islamic law derived from the Quran and Sunnah?
What is fiqh in Islamic legal terminology?
Fiqh is Islamic jurisprudence — the practical rulings derived by scholars from the sources of Sharia.
What are the four main sources of Islamic law (usul al-fiqh)?
The Quran, the Sunnah (Hadith), Ijma (scholarly consensus), and Qiyas (analogical reasoning).
What is a fatwa in Islamic law?
A formal legal opinion or ruling issued by a qualified Islamic scholar (mufti) on a religious or legal question.
What legal system is based on the Napoleonic Code and is used in many Arab countries?
Civil law (code law) system, as inherited from French or Egyptian civil codes.
What is the Arabic term for the fixed punishments prescribed by Islamic law for specific offenses?
Hudud (حدود) — the set of specific punishments for crimes like theft, slander, and highway robbery.
What is the Islamic legal principle of qisas?
Qisas is the principle of proportional retaliation ('an eye for an eye') in cases of murder or bodily harm, where the victim's family may choose retaliation, blood money, or forgiveness.
What is the Arabic legal term for a Muslim marriage contract?
Aqd al-nikah (عقد النكاح) — the marriage contract requiring offer, acceptance, two witnesses, and a dowry (mahr).
What is the mahr in Islamic marriage law?
A mandatory gift or payment made by the groom to the bride, which becomes her exclusive property.
What is the Arabic term for the waiting period a woman must observe after divorce or a husband's death before remarrying?
Iddah (عدة) — typically three menstrual cycles after divorce, or four months and ten days after a husband's death.
What is a waqf in Islamic law?
A waqf is a religious endowment — property donated for charitable, religious, or educational purposes, which cannot be sold or transferred.
What is the science of Islamic inheritance law called?
Ilm al-faraidh (علم الفرائض) — the science of prescribed inheritance shares defined in the Quran.
What does the term 'sovereignty' mean in international law?
The exclusive authority of a state to govern itself, make laws, and conduct affairs within its territory without interference from other states.
What does the Latin phrase 'presumption of innocence' mean in criminal law?
A defendant is considered innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt — the prosecution bears the burden of proof.
What country has the largest and most influential civil code in the Arab world, widely adopted by other nations?
Egypt — the Egyptian Civil Code (1949), drafted by Abd El-Razzak El-Sanhuri, was adopted as the basis for civil law in Iraq, Syria, Libya, Kuwait, and others.
What are the five categories of acts in Islamic law (ahkam al-khamsa)?
Wajib (obligatory), Mandub (recommended), Mubah (permissible), Makruh (discouraged), and Haram (forbidden).
What are the four major Sunni schools of Islamic jurisprudence (madhabs)?
The Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali schools, each named after its founding scholar.
What are the essential elements of a valid contract in most Arab civil law systems?
Offer and acceptance (meeting of minds), legal capacity of the parties, a lawful object, and a lawful cause (consideration).
What is the Arab League and what legal role does it play in the region?

Founded in 1945, the Arab League is a regional organization of Arab states that promotes cooperation and coordinates policy. It adopts resolutions and conventions, though its legal instruments are generally non-binding on member states without domestic ratification.
What constitutional provision is common to Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE regarding the basis of their legal systems?
All three designate Islamic Sharia as a (or the) principal source of legislation in their constitutional documents.
What is ta'zir in Islamic criminal law?
Discretionary punishments imposed by a judge for offenses not covered by hudud or qisas, where the punishment type and severity is left to judicial discretion.
What is riba in Islamic law and how is it defined?

Riba (ربا) means any increase or excess charged over a loan principal — broadly interpreted as interest. It is prohibited in Islam. Islamic finance uses profit-sharing instruments (mudarabah, musharakah) to achieve similar economic outcomes without charging fixed interest.
What is the difference between talaq and khul' in Islamic divorce law?

Talaq is divorce initiated by the husband by pronouncing the divorce formula. Khul' is divorce initiated by the wife, who typically returns the mahr (dowry) to the husband in exchange for release from the marriage.
What is a sukuk in Islamic finance?

Sukuk are Islamic financial certificates representing ownership stakes in assets or projects — the Islamic equivalent of bonds. They generate returns through profit-sharing or rent from the underlying asset rather than interest payments.
What is the kafala (sponsorship) system common in Gulf states and how does it affect migrant workers?

The kafala system ties a migrant worker's legal residency and employment to a specific local sponsor (kafeel). Workers cannot change employers or leave the country without sponsor permission, creating dependency and vulnerability to exploitation. Several Gulf states have begun reforming or dismantling the system.
What is the principle of non-intervention in international law?

The principle that states are forbidden from intervening in the internal affairs of other sovereign states — enshrined in Article 2(1) of the UN Charter. It prohibits coercive interference in political, economic, or social matters.
What is the Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam (1990)?

Adopted by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), it affirms human rights but subordinates them to Islamic Sharia, offering an alternative framework to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It is criticized for limiting rights to what Sharia permits.
What is the burden of proof for hudud crimes in classical Islamic jurisprudence?

Extremely high — for example, zina (adultery/fornication) requires four male witnesses to the act itself. This effectively made enforcement rare in classical fiqh, with scholars arguing the strict standard was intended to limit actual punishment.
What is murabaha in Islamic finance and how is it used for home or car purchases?

Murabaha is a cost-plus financing arrangement: the bank buys an asset outright and resells it to the customer at a disclosed markup, payable in installments. This avoids interest while achieving similar financing outcomes.
What is the difference between a presidential and a parliamentary system of government?

In a presidential system (e.g. USA, Egypt), the executive is separate from the legislature and directly elected. In a parliamentary system (e.g. UK, Jordan), the executive (prime minister) is drawn from and accountable to the legislature.
What is the principle of jus cogens in international law?
Peremptory norms of international law from which no derogation is permitted — such as the prohibitions on genocide, slavery, and torture. They cannot be overridden by treaty.
What is the Islamic concept of wilaya in family law?

Wilaya is guardianship or protective authority — most commonly the male guardian's (wali) role in a woman's marriage, which classical fiqh requires for the marriage contract's validity. Contemporary Muslim-majority states vary widely in how strictly they apply this requirement.
What is ijara in Islamic finance?

Ijara is an Islamic leasing contract where a bank or financier buys an asset and leases it to the customer for an agreed rental, with ownership optionally transferring at the end. It is used for vehicle and equipment financing as an interest-free alternative.
What is the diya (blood money) system in Islamic law?

Diya is financial compensation paid to the victim or victim's family in cases of unintentional killing or bodily harm, as an alternative to qisas retaliation. Amounts vary by injury type and are still applied in several Muslim-majority legal systems.
What is the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and what types of cases does it hear?

The principal judicial organ of the UN, based in The Hague. It settles legal disputes between states (contentious cases) and gives advisory opinions on legal questions referred by UN organs. Only states — not individuals — can be parties to contentious cases.
What is the Arab Charter on Human Rights?

A human rights instrument adopted by the Arab League in 2004, entering into force in 2008. It guarantees civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights, but is criticized for allowing derogation on national security grounds and for not fully aligning with international standards.
What is the role of the Constitutional Court in Egypt's legal system?

Egypt's Supreme Constitutional Court has exclusive jurisdiction over the constitutionality of legislation, interprets legislative texts referred to it, and settles jurisdictional conflicts between courts. Its rulings are final and binding on all state organs.
What is the Wage Protection System (WPS) used in UAE and Saudi Arabia?

An electronic salary monitoring system that requires employers to pay workers' wages through approved financial channels on time. Compliance is tracked by authorities, and non-paying employers face fines, work permit bans, or criminal prosecution.
What is ijtihad in Islamic law and why was it historically controversial?

Ijtihad is independent legal reasoning to derive new rulings on matters not explicitly addressed in the Quran or Sunnah. It became controversial after classical scholars declared 'the closing of the gate of ijtihad' — suggesting most major legal questions had been settled — though this view is contested and modern reformists strongly advocate reopening ijtihad.
What is arbitration and why is it commonly used in international commercial contracts in the Middle East?

Arbitration is a private dispute resolution process where parties agree to submit disputes to one or more arbitrators whose decision (award) is binding. In international trade, it is preferred over national courts because it is neutral, confidential, and awards are enforceable internationally under the New York Convention (1958).
What is the difference between a crime and a tort in most Arab civil law systems?

A crime is a wrong against society prosecuted by the state, resulting in criminal penalties (imprisonment, fines). A tort (civil wrong) is a wrong against an individual that gives rise to a private civil action for compensation. The same act can constitute both a crime and a tort simultaneously.
What is the difference between ownership and possession in Arab civil law?

Ownership (milkiyya) is the full legal right to use, enjoy, and dispose of property. Possession (hiyaza) is the physical control of property, which may exist without ownership (e.g. a tenant possesses but doesn't own). Possession can give rise to certain legal protections even without full title.
How do dual legal systems (mixed sharia-civil law) function in countries like Egypt, Jordan, and Kuwait?

These countries apply civil law codes (French-derived) for commercial and criminal matters while applying Sharia in personal status law (marriage, divorce, inheritance, guardianship). Separate courts (personal status or sharia courts) handle family matters, while civil and criminal courts handle the rest. Integration is complex — Sharia principles often inform constitutional interpretation even in the civil domain.
What is the doctrine of maslaha (public interest) in Islamic jurisprudence and how has it been used in legal reform?

Maslaha holds that rulings may be derived or reformed to serve the public good, even if not explicitly derived from Quran or Sunnah texts, provided they do not contradict established principles. Reformist scholars use it to argue for updating Islamic law on issues like women's rights, banking, and criminal penalties to fit modern contexts.
What is the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) doctrine and how has it been applied in the Arab world?

R2P holds that states have a primary responsibility to protect their populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity. When a state fails, the international community may intervene. It was controversially invoked for the 2011 NATO intervention in Libya (UNSC Resolution 1973), raising debates about its limits and potential for misuse.
What is the concept of shura in Islamic political theory and how do Gulf states incorporate it into governance?

Shura is the principle of consultation — rulers should consult with advisors or representatives before making decisions. Gulf states incorporate it through consultative councils (like Saudi Arabia's Majlis al-Shura or Qatar's Majlis) that advise the ruler but lack full legislative power, representing a partial institutionalization of shura principles.
What is the role of a Sharia Supervisory Board in Islamic banking?

A Sharia Supervisory Board is a panel of qualified Islamic scholars who review and certify that a bank's financial products, contracts, and operations comply with Sharia principles. They issue fatwas on products and audit transactions. Their independence and consistency across institutions remains a subject of debate in Islamic finance governance.
What are the Rome Statute and the International Criminal Court (ICC), and why have some Arab states not ratified them?

The Rome Statute (1998) established the ICC, the first permanent international criminal court with jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Many Arab states have not ratified it due to concerns about sovereignty, potential politically motivated prosecutions, and the ICC's previous focus on African and Middle Eastern situations. The ratio between the toxic dose and the effective dose (TD50/ED50). A wide therapeutic index means a drug is relatively safe; a narrow therapeutic index (e.g. warfarin, lithium, digoxin) means small dose changes can cause toxicity or loss of effect.
What is the mechanism of action of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like omeprazole?
PPIs irreversibly block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) in gastric parietal cells, stopping acid secretion. They treat peptic ulcers, GERD, and H. pylori infections.
What is the mechanism of action of penicillin-class antibiotics?

Penicillins inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by blocking transpeptidase enzymes (penicillin-binding proteins), preventing cross-linking of peptidoglycan chains. This weakens the cell wall, causing the bacterium to burst (lyse).
What is the 'first-pass effect' and which drugs are most affected by it?

When an orally administered drug is absorbed through the gut and passes through the portal vein to the liver before reaching systemic circulation, much of it is metabolized — reducing bioavailability. Highly metabolized drugs like morphine, nitroglycerin, and lidocaine show significant first-pass effects and may need higher oral doses or alternative routes.
What are SSRIs and what are they primarily used to treat?

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors block reuptake of serotonin in synapses, increasing serotonin availability. They are the first-line treatment for depression and anxiety disorders (e.g. fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram).
What is the WHO's ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical) classification system?

A system for classifying drugs by the organ or body system they act on and their therapeutic, pharmacological, and chemical properties — organized in five levels. It is used globally for drug utilization research and comparison.
What is heparin and how does it work as an anticoagulant?

Heparin is an injectable anticoagulant that activates antithrombin III, which then rapidly inactivates thrombin and factor Xa — key enzymes in the clotting cascade. Used to prevent and treat blood clots (DVT, pulmonary embolism).
What is receptor downregulation and what clinical problem can it cause?

When a receptor is chronically activated (by an agonist drug), the cell reduces the number of available receptors. This causes drug tolerance — the same dose produces a weaker effect over time, requiring dose escalation. It is a major issue with opioids and beta-agonists in asthma.
What is volume of distribution (Vd) and what does a high Vd indicate?

Vd is a theoretical volume relating the total amount of drug in the body to its plasma concentration (Vd = total drug / plasma concentration). A high Vd means the drug distributes extensively into tissues and is not confined to plasma — making it harder to remove by dialysis. Lipophilic drugs (e.g. chloroquine, amiodarone) have very high Vd values.
What is the difference between bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics and does it matter clinically?

Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria (e.g. penicillins, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides); bacteriostatic antibiotics inhibit growth, relying on immune clearance (e.g. tetracyclines, macrolides, sulfonamides). In immunocompromised patients or endocarditis, bactericidal drugs are preferred because the immune system cannot finish the job.
What is Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) in drug safety?

A rare but life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction causing blistering and peeling of skin and mucous membranes. Commonly triggered by drugs including carbamazepine, allopurinol, lamotrigine, sulfonamides, and NSAIDs. It requires immediate discontinuation of the offending drug and intensive supportive care.
What is the mechanism of action of metformin in type 2 diabetes?

Metformin primarily activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) in the liver, inhibiting gluconeogenesis (glucose production) and reducing hepatic glucose output. It also improves insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues. It does not cause hypoglycemia and is weight-neutral.
What is the difference between Phase I and Phase II drug metabolism?

Phase I reactions (mainly by CYP450 enzymes in liver) introduce or unmask functional groups (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) — often activating prodrugs or making drugs more polar. Phase II reactions conjugate the drug or Phase I metabolite with endogenous molecules (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation) to make them more water-soluble for excretion.
What is the mechanism of warfarin and why does it require careful monitoring?

Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of vitamin K — essential for producing clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. Its effect is measured by INR. It has a narrow therapeutic index, is affected by diet (vitamin K foods) and many drug interactions (especially CYP2C9 inhibitors/inducers), requiring regular dose adjustment.
What is the difference between tolerance, dependence, and addiction in the context of opioid drugs?

Tolerance: reduced drug effect with repeated use, requiring higher doses. Physical dependence: physiological adaptation where abrupt cessation causes withdrawal syndrome. Addiction: compulsive drug-seeking behavior despite harmful consequences — a neurological disease. All three can coexist; tolerance and dependence can occur without addiction.
What is the difference between drug toxicity and drug allergy?

Drug toxicity is a dose-dependent, pharmacologically predictable harmful effect (e.g. acetaminophen overdose causing liver failure). Drug allergy is an immune-mediated reaction (hypersensitivity) that can occur at any dose, is unpredictable from pharmacology, and requires prior sensitization — ranging from mild rash to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
What is the mechanism of aminoglycoside antibiotics and what is their main toxicity?

Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin) irreversibly bind the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and production of faulty proteins — killing bacteria. Their main toxicities are nephrotoxicity (kidney damage) and ototoxicity (hearing/balance damage), which are dose-related and cumulative.
What is the concept of 'therapeutic drug monitoring' (TDM) and which drug classes benefit most?

TDM is the practice of measuring drug concentrations in blood to optimize dosing. Most useful for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index and high inter-patient variability: aminoglycosides, vancomycin, lithium, phenytoin, digoxin, cyclosporine, and tacrolimus.
What is pharmacogenomics and how can CYP2D6 polymorphisms affect drug therapy?

Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation affects drug response. CYP2D6 metabolizes ~25% of drugs (codeine, tamoxifen, many antidepressants). Poor metabolizers accumulate drug, risking toxicity; ultra-rapid metabolizers clear it too fast, losing efficacy. Codeine in ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers converts to dangerous morphine levels — an FDA-labeled risk.
What is the difference between zero-order and first-order drug elimination kinetics?

First-order kinetics: a constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit time (most drugs) — concentration-time curve is exponential. Zero-order kinetics: a constant amount is eliminated per unit time regardless of concentration (e.g. ethanol, phenytoin at high doses) — because eliminating enzymes are saturated. Zero-order kinetics causes disproportionate toxicity with dose escalation.
What are the four phases of clinical drug trials?

Phase I: safety, tolerability, PK/PD in small healthy volunteers. Phase II: efficacy and safety in small patient populations, dose-finding. Phase III: large randomized controlled trials confirming efficacy and safety vs. placebo/standard care — required for regulatory approval. Phase IV: post-marketing surveillance for long-term or rare adverse effects.
What is the concept of 'targeted therapy' in oncology and how do tyrosine kinase inhibitors work?

Targeted therapy attacks specific molecular abnormalities in cancer cells rather than killing all rapidly dividing cells. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) like imatinib (Gleevec) block overactive kinase enzymes (e.g. BCR-ABL in CML) that drive cancer cell proliferation. They are more selective and often have fewer side effects than traditional chemotherapy.
What are the main molecular mechanisms by which bacteria develop antibiotic resistance?

1. Enzymatic inactivation (e.g. beta-lactamases destroying penicillins). 2. Target modification (altered penicillin-binding proteins in MRSA). 3. Efflux pumps (actively expelling antibiotic from cell). 4. Reduced permeability (decreased outer membrane porins). 5. Target bypass (alternative metabolic pathways). Resistance genes can transfer between bacteria via plasmids (horizontal gene transfer).
What is the difference between a competitive reversible antagonist and a non-competitive irreversible antagonist?

A competitive reversible antagonist competes with the agonist for the same binding site — its effect can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration (the dose-response curve shifts right but maximum effect is maintained). A non-competitive/irreversible antagonist binds covalently or at an allosteric site, and its effect cannot be overcome by more agonist — maximum effect is reduced even at high agonist doses.
What is 'prodrug design' and give a clinically important example?

A prodrug is an inactive compound that is converted in the body to its active form. Prodrug design improves bioavailability, stability, or reduces toxicity. Example: Enalapril is an ester prodrug of enalaprilat — the active ACE inhibitor — because enalaprilat is poorly absorbed orally but enalapril's ester is absorbed well and hydrolyzed to enalaprilat after absorption.
What are monoclonal antibodies and how are they used as drugs?

Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are laboratory-produced antibodies that bind a specific target (antigen) with high precision. As drugs, they can block disease-causing proteins (e.g. trastuzumab blocks HER2 in breast cancer; adalimumab blocks TNF-α in rheumatoid arthritis; rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells in lymphoma). They often have suffix -mab in their name.
What is the concept of 'mechanism-based inhibition' (suicide inhibition) of CYP450 enzymes?

Some drugs are metabolized by CYP450 enzymes into reactive intermediates that permanently inactivate the enzyme — 'committing suicide.' This causes irreversible drug interactions lasting until new enzyme is synthesized (days–weeks). Examples: erythromycin (CYP3A4), isoniazid (CYP2E1), grapefruit furanocoumarins (CYP3A4 in gut wall). Drug levels of CYP3A4 substrates can rise dramatically when grapefruit is consumed.
What is 'biopharmaceutics classification system' (BCS) and how does it guide drug formulation?

The BCS classifies drugs by aqueous solubility and intestinal permeability into 4 classes: I (high solubility, high permeability — ideal), II (low solubility, high permeability — formulation key to improving dissolution), III (high solubility, low permeability — absorption enhancement needed), IV (low solubility, low permeability — most challenging). BCS guides whether modified-release or special delivery systems are needed for adequate bioavailability.
What is the mechanism of action of checkpoint inhibitors in cancer immunotherapy?

Tumor cells evade immune destruction by expressing inhibitory checkpoint proteins (PD-L1, CTLA-4) that suppress T-cell activity. Checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. nivolumab, pembrolizumab block PD-1; ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4) remove these brakes, allowing T cells to recognize and kill cancer cells. This can cause immune-related adverse effects in normal tissues.
What are lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and why were they critical to mRNA vaccine delivery?

Lipid nanoparticles are tiny spherical vesicles made of lipids that encapsulate and protect mRNA from degradation and facilitate its delivery into cells. They fuse with cell membranes, releasing mRNA into the cytoplasm. This technology, developed over decades, was essential for COVID-19 mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna) — solving the major challenge that naked mRNA is rapidly degraded in the body.
What is the difference between pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic drug tolerance?

Pharmacokinetic tolerance: the body metabolizes or excretes the drug faster over time (enzyme induction), reducing plasma levels after the same dose. Pharmacodynamic tolerance: the drug concentration is unchanged but the target response is reduced — via receptor downregulation, desensitization, or compensatory physiological changes. Both mechanisms can contribute simultaneously.
What is PBPK (physiologically based pharmacokinetic) modelling and what is its value in drug development?

PBPK models use mathematical equations representing actual organ volumes, blood flows, and biochemical processes to simulate drug distribution and elimination throughout the whole body. They can predict drug behavior in special populations (children, pregnant women, patients with renal/hepatic impairment) without exposing them to the drug — reducing costly animal studies and informing regulatory submissions for dose adjustment recommendations.
Which Athenian philosopher is associated with a method of questioning explored in many of Plato’s dialogues?
What is Plato's theory of Forms?

Plato argued that the physical world is an imperfect copy of a higher realm of perfect, eternal abstract entities called Forms or Ideas. For example, all beautiful things participate in the Form of Beauty itself, which exists independently of any physical example.
What is Aristotle's concept of the 'Golden Mean'?

The ethical principle that virtue lies between two extremes (excess and deficiency). For example, courage is the mean between cowardice (deficiency) and recklessness (excess). This is part of his virtue ethics framework.
What is René Descartes' most famous philosophical statement?
'Cogito, ergo sum' — 'I think, therefore I am.' It was his foundational certainty: even if everything else could be doubted, the very act of doubting proves the existence of a thinking subject.
A family of ethical theories that evaluates actions by their consequences for overall welfare or utility. Maximizing total utility is not always the same as benefiting the largest headcount.
What is Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative?

Kant's supreme principle of morality: 'Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.' In other words, only do what you could will everyone to do.

The branch of philosophy that studies the nature, sources, scope, and limits of knowledge. Key questions: What is knowledge? How do we know anything? What is the difference between belief and justified belief?
What is the mind-body problem in philosophy?
The problem of how mental experience relates to the physical body and brain. Different theories disagree about whether mental states are physical, nonphysical or understood in another way.
What did Plato's allegory of the cave illustrate?

Prisoners in a cave see only shadows on a wall and think this is reality. When one escapes and sees the real world and sun, he returns to tell the others who refuse to believe him. It illustrates how most people mistake appearances for reality, and how true knowledge requires philosophical 'enlightenment'.
What is the social contract theory associated with Locke, Hobbes, and Rousseau?

The theory that legitimate political authority derives from an agreement (explicit or implicit) among individuals to form a society and give up certain freedoms to a government in exchange for security and social order.
An ancient philosophical school associated with Zeno of Citium, emphasizing virtue, judgment and distinguishing what is within our control from what is not.

An error in reasoning that makes an argument invalid or misleading. Examples: ad hominem (attacking the person rather than the argument), straw man (misrepresenting an opponent's argument), false dichotomy (presenting only two options when more exist).
What is the trolley problem in ethics?

A thought experiment about diverting a runaway trolley from several people toward one person. It explores tensions between consequences, duties and responsibility; the quiz identifies the problem, not a mandatory moral choice.
Who was Ibn Rushd (Averroes) and why was he significant in the history of philosophy?

Ibn Rushd (1126–1198) was an Andalusian Muslim philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle. His work transmitted Aristotle's philosophy to medieval Europe, influencing Aquinas and scholasticism. He argued for the compatibility of reason and faith, believing philosophy and theology could be reconciled.
What is the Gettier problem in epistemology?
Edmund Gettier’s counterexamples challenge whether justified true belief is sufficient for knowledge: a belief may be justified and true partly through luck.
What is the difference between deontological and consequentialist ethics?

Deontological ethics (Kant) judges actions as right or wrong based on whether they follow moral rules or duties — regardless of consequences. Consequentialist ethics (utilitarianism) judges actions by their outcomes — an action is right if it produces good consequences.
What is John Rawls' 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment?

Rawls asked: what principles of justice would rational people choose if they didn't know their own position in society (their wealth, class, race, talents)? Behind this 'veil of ignorance,' he argued, people would choose equal basic liberties and arrange inequalities to benefit the least advantaged — his 'difference principle.'
What is Leibniz's principle of the identity of indiscernibles?

The principle that if two things are indistinguishable in all their properties, they are in fact the same thing. In other words, there cannot be two numerically distinct objects that are qualitatively identical in every respect.
Which book did Ibn Rushd write in response to Al-Ghazali’s The Incoherence of the Philosophers?
The Incoherence of the Incoherence (Tahafut al-Tahafut). The exchange was through texts, not a meeting between the two men.
What is Karl Popper's criterion of falsifiability?

Popper proposed that a scientific theory should be open to possible refutation by observations or tests. This is his influential demarcation proposal, not an uncontested complete definition of science.
What is virtue ethics and how does it differ from Kantian ethics?

Virtue ethics emphasizes character and practical wisdom; Kantian ethics emphasizes duty and moral principles. This is a contrast in emphasis, not a claim that either ignores actions or character entirely.
What is Hume's problem of induction?

Hume argued that inductive reasoning (inferring general laws from observed cases — e.g. 'the sun has always risen, therefore it will rise tomorrow') cannot be logically justified. We have no rational basis to assume the future will resemble the past — we rely on habit and custom, not reason. This challenges the foundations of science and causation.
What is the 'hard problem of consciousness' described by David Chalmers?

The hard problem asks why physical brain processes give rise to subjective, first-person experience (qualia) — the 'what it is like' to see red, feel pain, or hear music. The 'easy problems' (explaining cognitive functions) seem tractable in principle; the hard problem — why any physical process produces inner experience at all — may be fundamentally beyond materialist explanation.
What is Peter Singer's argument for effective altruism?

Singer argues that if we can prevent something bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it — regardless of distance. This leads to the conclusion that wealthy people in developed countries have a strong moral obligation to give significantly to reduce extreme global poverty, since geographic distance has no moral relevance.
What is the ship of Theseus paradox?

It asks whether a ship remains the same ship as its parts are replaced, and what happens if the original parts form another ship. It is a problem of identity through change, not a settled biological claim.
Which philosopher is associated with the concept “will to power”?
What is Thomas Kuhn's concept of scientific paradigm shifts?

Kuhn distinguished normal science within a shared paradigm from scientific revolutions that change that framework. His account includes both puzzle-solving within paradigms and periods of fundamental change.
What is the ontological argument for God's existence and who formulated it?

Formulated by Anselm of Canterbury (11th century): God is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived.' If God existed only in the mind, something greater (one that also exists in reality) could be conceived — contradiction. Therefore God must exist in reality. Kant famously criticized it: 'existence is not a predicate.'
For a consistent, effectively axiomatized formal theory strong enough to express elementary arithmetic, what limitation does Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem establish?
Such a theory is incomplete: there is an arithmetic statement it can neither prove nor refute. The conclusion depends on those assumptions and is not a claim that all mathematical reasoning fails.
What is the naturalistic fallacy in ethics, identified by G.E. Moore?

Moore challenged defining good in terms of another property, using the open-question argument: it can still be meaningful to ask whether that property is good. His position is a philosophical argument, not an uncontested fact.
What is Ibn Sina's (Avicenna's) 'floating man' thought experiment?
Ibn Sina asks whether a newly created person without sensory contact would still be aware of their own existence. He argues yes, using this to support his account of self-awareness and the soul.
What is Wittgenstein's private language argument?

The late Wittgenstein argued that a 'private language' — one that refers to inner experiences only the speaker can access — is impossible. Language requires public criteria for correct usage; without the possibility of public checking, there is no difference between 'using a word correctly' and 'thinking one is using it correctly.' This challenges Cartesian privacy of mind.
What is Hannah Arendt's concept of the 'banality of evil'?

Arendt used the phrase when interpreting Eichmann’s trial, emphasizing thoughtlessness and bureaucratic compliance in grave wrongdoing. It should not be turned into a universal claim that every evil act has one simple cause.
What is the principle of sufficient reason (PSR)?
A principle associated with Leibniz that things or facts have a sufficient reason or explanation. Philosophers disagree about its scope and whether it admits exceptions or unexplained basic facts.
What is the paradox of the heap (sorites paradox)?
Removing one grain seems unable to turn a heap into a non-heap, but repeating the step eventually leaves no heap. The puzzle concerns vague boundaries; competing theories offer different responses.
What is the is-ought problem identified by David Hume?

Hume observed that many moral arguments make an unjustified jump from descriptive facts ('is') to normative conclusions ('ought'). From 'humans evolved to be social' you cannot derive 'humans ought to behave socially' without additional premises. This gap — the is-ought gap — is a foundational challenge in metaethics.
What is Sartre's concept of 'existence precedes essence'?

Sartre argued that humans are not born with a predetermined nature or purpose (essence). We exist first, then create our own essence through choices and actions. This is radically liberating but also terrifying — we are 'condemned to be free' and fully responsible for who we become.
Does Bostrom’s simulation argument claim to prove that we certainly live in a simulation?

No. Under its assumptions, it argues that at least one of three propositions holds, involving civilizations' survival, their simulation activity, or the prevalence of simulated observers. It does not establish which alternative is true.
In philosophy of mind, what defines a mental state according to functionalism?
Its functional or causal role: its relations to inputs, other mental states and outputs, rather than a specific physical material alone.
How does moral particularism contrast with moral generalism?
Moral particularism holds that a consideration’s moral relevance can change with context. Moral generalism gives moral principles a more central role in explaining or determining judgments.
What is epistemic injustice and what are its two main forms as described by Miranda Fricker?

Epistemic injustice is a wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower. Miranda Fricker identifies: (1) Testimonial injustice — giving a speaker deflated credibility due to identity prejudice (e.g. disbelieving someone because of their gender or race); (2) Hermeneutical injustice — having inadequate conceptual resources to understand one's own experience (e.g. having no concept for 'sexual harassment' before it was named).
Compare “Necessarily, the winner is a winner” with “This actual winner could not have lost.” Which claim places necessity on the proposition, and which on a particular person?
The first is de dicto: necessity applies to the proposition. The second is de re: it attributes a necessary property to a particular person. The second does not follow from the first.
What is the Duhem-Quine thesis in philosophy of science?

The thesis that scientific hypotheses cannot be tested in isolation — any test involves auxiliary hypotheses (background assumptions, instrument calibration, ceteris paribus conditions). When a prediction fails, we cannot know if the main hypothesis is wrong or one of the auxiliaries is at fault. This means no single experiment can definitively refute a theory — only a whole web of beliefs can be tested as a unit.
What is the difference between negative and positive liberty as described by Isaiah Berlin?

Negative liberty: freedom from external constraints and interference (the absence of obstacles). Positive liberty: freedom to actually pursue one's goals and realize one's potential — which may require resources and conditions. Berlin warned that positive liberty can be co-opted by authoritarian regimes to justify imposing a 'true' freedom on citizens.
What is the repugnant conclusion in population ethics (Derek Parfit)?

The implication, under total-welfare comparisons, that a sufficiently large population with lives barely worth living can rank above a smaller very happy population. Parfit used it to expose a difficult problem in population ethics.
What is Kripke's causal theory of reference and how does it challenge Frege-Russell descriptivism?

Frege-Russell descriptivism held that proper names refer by being associated with descriptions (Aristotle = 'the teacher of Alexander'). Kripke argued names are 'rigid designators' — they refer to the same object in all possible worlds, regardless of which descriptions are true. Reference is fixed causally: an initial baptism creates a chain of communication. Names still refer even when all believed descriptions are false.
What is the separateness of persons objection to utilitarianism?

Rawls and Nozick argued that utilitarianism fails to take seriously the fact that people are distinct individuals. Maximizing aggregate welfare can justify sacrificing one person for the benefit of many — treating people as mere vessels of utility rather than ends in themselves. This fails to respect the separateness of persons — you cannot compensate my suffering with someone else's happiness, because they are not the same person.
What is the debate between presentism and eternalism in the philosophy of time?

Presentism holds that only the present moment exists — the past is gone and the future does not yet exist. Eternalism (block universe theory) holds that all times — past, present, and future — are equally real and co-exist in a four-dimensional spacetime block. Eternalism is compatible with special relativity (which shows simultaneity is relative), while presentism struggles to accommodate relativity theory.
What is structural realism in philosophy of science and how does it respond to the pessimistic meta-induction?

Structural realism argues that some relational or mathematical structure can be preserved through theory change, responding to worries raised by the failure of past successful theories. This is a philosophical response, not proof that all structure survives.
What is the distinction between agent-relative and agent-neutral reasons in ethics?
Agent-neutral reasons apply independently of the agent’s identity; agent-relative reasons can depend on that person’s commitments or relationships, such as special obligations to their own child.
What is the speed of light in a vacuum?
What region of a bacterial cell contains its chromosome?
The nucleoid. Unlike a eukaryotic nucleus, it is not enclosed by a membrane.
In an aqueous solution, which substance is the solvent?
Water. The term aqueous means that a substance is dissolved in water.
Which blood components form the initial plug that helps stop bleeding?
Platelets. They adhere to damaged blood vessels and aggregate to form a platelet plug.
How are the frequency f and period T of a repeating wave related?
They are reciprocals: f = 1/T. A longer period therefore means a lower frequency.
What is the most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere?
What molecule carries genetic information in living cells?
Which type of lens brings parallel light rays to a focus?
What is the pH of a neutral solution at 25 °C?
How do root hairs help a plant absorb water and minerals?
They greatly increase the root's surface area in contact with the soil.
According to Newton's first law, what happens to an object at rest if no net force acts on it?
It remains at rest (law of inertia).
What property of minerals is ranked by the Mohs scale?
Scratch hardness: resistance to being scratched by another material.
Which molecule serves as the immediate energy currency of cells?
ATP (adenosine triphosphate). Cells release usable energy when ATP is hydrolyzed.
What does Einstein's famous equation E = mc² represent?
Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared — mass and energy are equivalent and interconvertible.
What is Avogadro's number and what does it represent?
6.022 × 10²³; it is the number of atoms, molecules, or ions in one mole of a substance.
Starting with one diploid cell, how do the usual chromosome numbers of mitosis and meiosis products differ?
Mitosis preserves diploidy; meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce haploid products. Not all meiotic products necessarily become functional gametes.
The change in observed frequency of a wave when the source or observer is moving; e.g., a siren sounds higher-pitched as it approaches and lower as it recedes.
A reaction that releases heat energy to the surroundings, resulting in a negative ΔH.
The process by which organisms with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully, driving evolution over generations.
What is the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity?
A scalar has magnitude only, such as temperature. A vector has magnitude and direction, such as force or velocity.
What causes a rain shadow on the leeward side of a mountain range?
Moist air rises and rains on the windward side; the descending air on the leeward side warms and becomes drier.
What is the difference between ionic and covalent bonds?
An ionic bond is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. A covalent bond involves shared electron density, commonly represented by shared electron pairs.
What is the role of ribosomes in the cell?
Ribosomes synthesize proteins by translating messenger RNA (mRNA) into amino acid chains.
An object of mass 2 kg accelerates at 3 m/s². What net force acts on it?
If a system at equilibrium is disturbed (by changing concentration, pressure, or temperature), the equilibrium will shift to partially oppose the change.
What is the function of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in a eukaryotic cell?
The rough ER (studded with ribosomes) synthesizes and folds proteins; the smooth ER synthesizes lipids and detoxifies compounds.
What does Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle state?
It is impossible to simultaneously know both the exact position and exact momentum of a particle with arbitrary precision; Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2.
What is the difference between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion?
Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones (used in nuclear reactors); fusion merges light nuclei into heavier ones (powers the Sun). Both release enormous energy.
What is the usual sequence-information pathway during gene expression from DNA to protein?
DNA is transcribed into RNA, then messenger RNA is translated into protein: DNA→RNA→protein. This does not exclude reverse transcription from RNA to DNA.
What does the second law of thermodynamics say about the entropy of an isolated macroscopic system?
Its entropy cannot decrease in a spontaneous process; it increases in irreversible processes and remains constant in an ideal reversible process.
What is a catalyst and how does it speed up a reaction without being consumed?
A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It participates in intermediates but is regenerated by the end of the reaction.
What is allosteric regulation of an enzyme?
A regulator binds at a site other than the active site and changes the enzyme's activity by altering its shape.
Quantum objects (electrons, photons) exhibit both wave-like and particle-like behaviour depending on how they are observed. The double-slit experiment demonstrates this duality.
What is the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid?
In water, a strong acid such as HCl ionizes essentially completely. A weak acid such as acetic acid ionizes only partly and reaches an equilibrium with its conjugate base.
How does the CRISPR-Cas9 system work?
A guide RNA (gRNA) directs the Cas9 protein to a specific DNA sequence, where Cas9 makes a double-strand cut. The cell's repair mechanisms can then delete, correct, or insert genes.
What is the greenhouse effect and how does it cause climate change?

Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) trap infrared radiation re-emitted by Earth's surface. Increased anthropogenic emissions enhance this effect, raising global average temperatures and disrupting climate systems.
Why was the photoelectric effect important to the development of quantum theory?
Electron emission depends on a threshold light frequency. Einstein explained it using light quanta with energy E=hf, where classical wave theory alone could not explain the observations.
The study of heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve changes to the DNA sequence itself — caused by mechanisms such as DNA methylation and histone modification.
Can measurements of entangled particles be used to send a controllable message faster than light?
No. Entanglement produces nonclassical correlations, but comparing outcomes still requires ordinary communication subject to the light-speed limit.
If Ψ is an electron's normalized spatial wavefunction, what expression gives its position probability density?
|Ψ|²=Ψ*Ψ, where Ψ* is the complex conjugate. Ψ² alone is not generally correct.
What evidence supports the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts?
They retain their own genomes, bacterial-like ribosomes, and division mechanisms resembling bacteria, consistent with descent from bacterial ancestors living inside host cells.
Which bosons mediate the electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions in the Standard Model?
The photon mediates electromagnetism, W and Z bosons the weak interaction, and gluons the strong interaction. The Higgs boson is a separate scalar particle.
Why can two enantiomers of a chiral molecule have different biological effects?
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. Biological targets such as enzymes are also chiral, so the two forms may bind or react differently.
What is the role of telomeres in aging and cancer?

Telomeres are repetitive DNA caps protecting chromosome ends. They shorten with each cell division; when critically short, cells enter senescence or apoptosis. Cancer cells often upregulate telomerase to maintain telomere length and achieve replicative immortality.
What is the key difference between special and general relativity in their treatment of spacetime and gravity?
Special relativity describes physics in flat spacetime, including accelerated motion. General relativity describes gravity through curved spacetime shaped by mass-energy.
What is a Grignard reagent and how is it used in organic synthesis?

A Grignard reagent is an organomagnesium halide (RMgX) formed by reacting an alkyl or aryl halide with magnesium in dry ether. As a strong nucleophile/base, it attacks carbonyl groups (aldehydes, ketones, esters) to form new C–C bonds, enabling construction of complex alcohols.
What is apoptosis and how does the intrinsic pathway trigger it?

Apoptosis is programmed cell death. What characterizes a Bose–Einstein condensate in a dilute gas cooled to extremely low temperature?
A macroscopic fraction of the bosons occupies the same lowest-energy quantum state. Bosons have integer spin.
How do the basic mechanisms of SN1 and SN2 substitution differ?

SN1 forms a carbocation intermediate before nucleophile attack and often gives partial racemization. SN2 is concerted: backside attack and leaving-group departure occur together, with inversion at the reacting stereocenter.
What distinguishes synthetic biology from merely observing naturally occurring biological systems?

Perception organizes elements into wholes whose properties cannot be understood from isolated parts alone. A common summary is that the whole is different from the sum of its parts.

What is Maslow's hierarchy of needs?

Which mental-health profession requires training as a medical doctor: psychiatrist or psychologist?
Psychiatrist. Psychologists’ qualifications and permitted activities vary by jurisdiction; they are not necessarily medical doctors.

People remember items at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of a list better than those in the middle

What is Carl Jung's concept of the collective unconscious?
A layer of the unconscious shared across humanity, containing archetypes and universal symbols
What is Erikson's theory of psychosocial development?
Eight stages of development across the lifespan, each with a central conflict to resolve
What was the Milgram experiment about?
Obedience to authority — participants administered what they believed were dangerous electric shocks when instructed
Which six emotions appear in Paul Ekman’s commonly taught basic-emotion model?
Happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, anger and surprise. This identifies the model, not a claim that every theory uses the same classification.

What is Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD)?
The gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can achieve with guidance
People evaluate their own opinions and abilities by comparing themselves to others
What is the MBTI (Myers-Briggs Type Indicator)?
A personality questionnaire framework that describes 16 types using four preference pairs: E/I, S/N, T/F and J/P. Its types should not be treated as definitive diagnoses.

Which organization publishes the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, including DSM-5-TR?
What is the default mode network (DMN)?
A brain network active during rest, mind-wandering, and self-referential thinking
What is the fundamental attribution error?
Overestimating dispositional causes (character) and underestimating situational causes for others' behaviour
What is schema theory in cognitive psychology?
Mental frameworks organising and interpreting information based on prior experience

In reward-learning research, what is the difference between an expected reward and the reward actually received called?
A reward prediction error; activity in some dopamine pathways is associated with this signal.
What did Ainsworth’s Strange Situation procedure observe to study infant attachment?
Infants’ behavior during brief separations from and reunions with a caregiver in a structured setting.
What was the Stanford Prison Experiment?

A 1971 simulated-prison study led by Philip Zimbardo. It is historically influential, but methodological and ethical criticisms mean it should not be presented as conclusive proof of a universal effect of social roles.
Is “neurosis” a historical umbrella term or a single current DSM-5-TR diagnosis?
A historical umbrella term. It should not be treated as one current diagnosis equivalent to psychosis.
What does the term neurogenesis mean?
What is the difference between classical and operant conditioning?
Classical conditioning pairs stimuli to create involuntary responses; operant conditioning shapes voluntary behaviour through consequences
What is Kohlberg's theory of moral development?
Six stages in three levels: pre-conventional, conventional, and post-conventional moral reasoning
